mantra.line: Coordination is the serial part. Cut it to four handoffs and the parallel work actually runs in parallel.
Each specialist reads one source and writes one fragment. A narrow context has fewer ways to wander.
No peer checks. One reviewer at the merge, a script where a script can do it, catches most of what sixteen mutual checkers would.

paragraphs.name: Situation
paragraphs.plain: What you said, what the sit rep cost before, and what the doctrine changes.

strand.last: The gearbox capped the fleet at three; the sit rep still read everything on the main line.
strand.plan: Apply the doctrine to the one run that happens every session.
strand.you: You brought the math: Amdahl, Brooks, context as the cost unit, review at the merge.

items.t: **"Independent specialists, syncing only at defined handoff points, wins almost every time. Continuous cross-checking is the expensive part, not the work."**
**Amdahl:** parallel speedup is capped by the serial fraction, and coordination is the serial fraction. Sixteen agents reading each other is a sequential job with a sixteen-fold bill.
**Brooks:** channels grow n(n−1)/2. Sixteen agents talking is 120 channels; hub and spoke is 16.
**Context is the cost unit.** A narrow agent with three tools has a small prompt, cheaper calls, fewer ways to wander, less drift. The restriction is not the point; the smaller decision space is.
**Errors don't propagate across independent agents, but nobody catches them either.** So one reviewer at the fan-in, not a peer check on every step. Reviewing is far cheaper than generating.
**Mid-run sync only where outputs truly depend on each other.** A lot of that means the job was not decomposable; fewer agents in sequence would have been cheaper.

**One agent, the main line, on Fable:** read SOP · STATE · BOLO · PROJECTS · the cache (211 KB, about 55,000 tokens), wrote the whole 27 KB board JSON by hand, then carried all of it in context for the rest of the session.
**The 9/10 night board's own header says it:** three rounds, nine calls, ~75 KB read on the cheap path, more on a cold one. Sit rep and page sessions were 41% of the week.
**Two blocks never change between boards** (III is frozen since 8/15; VII is the proword list) and were rewritten every time.

paragraphs.task: Rebuild the sit rep as prep script → three independent specialists → script reviewer → the main line's one judgment,
paragraphs.intent: in order to cut the main line's read from about 211 KB to about 3 KB per board, move the reading onto haiku and sonnet contexts that end when they return, and make the same formation the Command rule for every fan-out.
paragraphs.spoken: "Orchestrator decomposes the job into pieces that don't share state, fans out to specialists who run independently, then fans in at a checkpoint where one agent reconciles and reviews."
endstate: "Sit rep" runs prep.py, three agents in one message, assemble.py, one main-line write, build, flush, publish.
The main line never opens STATE, BOLO, SOP, PROJECTS or the cache notes; it reads two digests.
The reviewer is a checklist in a script; advisory findings ride in the reply, blocking ones stop the write.
The formation rule sits in SOP §1 under the gear row and governs every multi-agent run.

paragraphs.main_effort: H2, the fan-in. The checklist is the reviewer; the main line's only judgment is Block VI and the header.

phases.t: **H0 · prep** — `python _tools/sitrep/prep.py`: the previous board split per block · STATE sliced to Blocked + Live (24 KB, not 74) · git log since the last board · box probe · III and VII carried · three briefs written. Zero tokens.

**H1 · fan out** — RACK (haiku: `_CACHE/` → Block 0) · INDEX (sonnet: STATE slices + git → I · II · V) · WATCH (haiku: BOLO.md → IV + PMCS), launched in one message, each reading only its brief's files, no cross-talk. Gear 1, no shift.

**H2 · fan in** — `assemble.py <date>`: merge · the reviewer's checklist (eight blocks in order · text + trunk on every item · glossary keys resolve · every BOLO number real and placed once · Block V rows = the Blocked table · plain + strand complete · no stale fragment) · the digest. The main line writes `frag/VI.json` and `meta.patch.json` off the digest.

**H3 · build, flush, publish** — `assemble.py <date> --build --flush` writes the board, builds SITREP.html, moves every cache note but today's to `_LOG/`; the Artifact tool republishes to the standing URL. The reply: link · Block 0 in three bullets · the leverage line · one caveat line.
**The first live run** — the next "sit rep". Read the findings; fix the one fragment that is wrong by rerunning its specialist with the finding pasted under the brief. Never launch a checker agent.

**The other three skills** — DOPE SHEET · FRAGO · Oscar Mike on the same pattern (BOLO 51, offload pick c). Oscar Mike is the natural second: one haiku writes the cache note from the transcript, a script appends the journal, the main line patches STATE.
